rv.q: Too much so, as it happens, in a mixed-bag of a production that despite some high points, struggles but fails to achieve a consistent tone.
The result feels more like an engaging gloss of The Cherry Orchard than the thing itself.
In the end, by stylizing Chekhov's world and rendering cultural details abstractly, the human stakes and basic relationships are drained of power.
Not that anyone really has a chance to shine in director Simon Godwin’s shapeless production.
But the much-anticipated production, with Diane Lane at the top of a blazingly promising cast, is perplexing, stylistic gibberish.
Many spectators must sigh in sympathy as they brave this disarrayed take on the Chekhov comedy, produced by the Roundabout Theater.
Those qualities are called for in the drama but seldom summoned in this dull, misconceived production.
This frenzied, flashy take on one family’s mortgage crisis may be the most clueless interpretation of Chekhov I have seen.
The result is a mixed bag lacking symbolic resonance: The audience gets neither the tragic grandeur nor the comedy of the aristocracy seeing its dominance end.
Yet from the start, the Roundabout Theatre Company's loud, broad revival makes no attempt to find a tragicomic balance.

"The Cherry Orchard," Chekhov's final play and a timeless tragicomedy about how people choose whether or not to respond to a changing world, proves to be less powerful than usual in the Roundabout Theatre Company's disjointed and flat revival, which stars Diane Lane alongside an accomplished ensemble.
The Roundabout’s production of THE CHERRY ORCHARD, as part of their 50th anniversary, is one of the pushed messes.
The result is a confused, flat and finally listless production.
In the end, they’re the least of what’s wrong in Simon Godwin’s staging of Stephen Karam’s new adaptation.
But a strong final 20 minutes does not save this Orchard from an over-pruning director.
Lane heads a wonderful ensemble cast in a production that gives most of them a chance to shine.

cn.t: This revival of Chekhov's classic earns largely negative reviews for its disjointed direction and flat staging. Critics find the production confused and shapeless, though a few praise its intimate approach and design elements.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'
